title: "CW-ERM: Improving Autonomous Driving Planning with Closed-loop Weighted Empirical Risk Minimization"

en.text: Most self-driving planners are trained by behavioral cloning: show the network what a human expert did, and ask it to reproduce the expert's next action. The training is done open-loop, one step at a time, matching expert actions on logged data. But when the policy actually drives, it runs closed-loop: every action it takes changes the state it sees next. A small steering error nudges the car into a slightly off-center position the expert never visited, the next prediction is a little worse, and the errors compound. This is covariate shift, and it is why a planner that looks excellent on open-loop metrics can still drift into collisions on the road.

There is a second, quieter problem. The metrics people actually care about (did the car collide, did it leave its lane) are non-differentiable. The training loss cannot see them directly, so open-loop training and closed-loop deployment end up optimizing two different objectives. The obvious remedy is to put a simulator inside the training loop and backpropagate through it, as methods like Urban Driver do. It works, but it is expensive: it needs a differentiable simulator, it does not scale well, and unrolling the policy during training is memory-hungry.

This NeurIPS 2022 paper from Woven Planet asks a simpler question. What if the simulator is used only to decide which training scenes matter, and never touches the loss function? Their answer is CW-ERM, or Closed-loop Weighted Empirical Risk Minimization: a two-step recipe that finds the scenes a policy fails on and upsamples exactly those scenes when training the final policy. The whole method is captured in the figure below.

en.caption: Figure 1. High-level overview of CW-ERM. Steps 1-2: train an identification policy with ordinary ERM. Step 3-4: roll it out in a closed-loop simulator and collect a cost metric (e.g. collisions) to build the error set. Steps 5-6: upsample the error-set scenes and retrain the final policy on the reweighted data.

en.text: Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.02174 · Code: https://github.com/wp-research-uk/cw-erm
Why open-loop training quietly hurts closed-loop driving

Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) is the standard behavioral-cloning objective: minimize the expected per-step imitation loss over states drawn from the expert's own distribution. The policy is only ever asked about states the expert visited, so it never learns to recover from its own mistakes. At deployment the distribution flips, since the states are now drawn from the policy's own rollouts, and the mismatch between these two distributions is precisely what makes the car unsafe. Because collisions are non-differentiable, the ERM loss offers no gradient that pushes the policy toward avoiding them. The authors' insight is that you do not need a gradient through the metric; you only need to know which scenes the policy gets wrong, and you can get that from a plain, non-differentiable simulator.
The method: three stages, one weighting term

CW-ERM is deliberately simple and breaks into three stages. First, train an identification policy the ordinary way, with standard ERM behavioral cloning. Second, roll that policy out in a closed-loop simulator across the training scenes and record a cost such as the number of collisions; every scene where the cost is positive, meaning every scene the policy fails, goes into an error set. Third, train the final policy again with weighted ERM, where the error-set scenes are upsampled by a factor w. The final objective is almost identical to plain behavioral cloning, with the single addition of a weight that is driven entirely by closed-loop failures.

Two practical details make it work. The identification policy is stopped early, after K epochs, so that it still fails often enough to populate a meaningful error set; train it to convergence and the error set is depleted. And rather than reweighting the loss, the authors physically upsample the failing scenes by an integer factor, which they find more stable. Because the simulator is used only to label scenes and never to compute a gradient, any non-differentiable metric can drive the weighting, and no differentiable simulator is needed. The paper also connects this reweight-by-failure scheme to the classic idea of correcting covariate shift through density-ratio estimation, giving the recipe a principled backbone.
Results: fewer collisions across the board

The method is evaluated on a proprietary real-world urban driving dataset collected by Woven Planet's self-driving cars on challenging missions in San Francisco and Palo Alto, complete with recorded ego and agent trajectories and HD maps. The scenes are hard and varied (stopping behind a lead vehicle, holding at intersections, threading dense traffic with pedestrians and cyclists) and run 11 to 13 seconds each, up to 30 seconds at the longest. Training uses 180 hours of driving, with 60 hours each held out for validation and test, and the final policy is trained for 40 epochs. The closed-loop simulator and metrics are released as open source.

Compared against the strongest baseline, behavioral cloning with ERM and expert perturbation, CW-ERM reduces collisions significantly across every metric, with improvements reaching about 35% on some of them. When the model upsamples front-collision scenes, front collisions fall from 14 to 9, roughly a 36% reduction. When it upsamples side-collision scenes, side collisions fall from 55 to 47. There is a welcome side effect: improving one metric often improves related ones. Upsampling side collisions also reduces rear collisions, a sign that the policy is becoming less passively cautious rather than gaming a single number. Variance is also lower than the baseline in several cases, so the gains are stable rather than lucky. Figure 2 shows the full picture across metrics and CW-ERM variants.

en.caption: Figure 2. Closed-loop evaluation across four collision metrics (front, side, rear, distance-to-reference). Each row is a CW-ERM variant that upsamples a different metric; the top row is the best baseline (ERM with perturbation). Bars show 0.95 confidence intervals from an exact Binomial posterior. Targeting a metric shrinks it, and improvements often carry over to related metrics.

en.text: The qualitative behavior is just as telling as the aggregate numbers. Figure 3 shows a test scene where the baseline drives into an intersection, ignores a car approaching from the right, and causes a front collision; the CW-ERM policy, trained with front-collision scenes upsampled, instead waits at the intersection until the path is clear. The change is not a cosmetic trajectory tweak: it is the policy learning to yield in exactly the situation type it used to fail on.

en.caption: Figure 3. A test scene, baseline (top) versus CW-ERM with front collisions upsampled (bottom), left to right in time. Blue dots are the target trajectory, yellow dots the prediction; the ego is the pink box, other agents the teal boxes. The baseline enters the intersection and collides with the car from the right (red arrow); CW-ERM waits instead.

en.text: How hard to upsample, and which metrics to combine

Two knobs govern how well the recipe works. The first is the upsampling factor w. Figure 4 sweeps it against side collisions on the validation set: performance improves steadily up to about w = 50, after which side collisions start to climb again, the same saturation the Just Train Twice (JTT) method reports for its upsampling scheme. The second knob is the early-stopping budget K of the identification policy: about 10 epochs works best for single-metric error sets and 20 for multi-metric ones. Together these give a small, legible search space rather than a fragile one.

en.caption: Figure 4. Side collisions on the validation set as a function of the upsampling factor w. Performance improves up to about w = 50 and degrades beyond it; the shaded band is the confidence interval.

en.text: There is also a choice of which failures to target. Upsampling a single metric gives the largest gain on that metric, while combining metrics trades them off along a Pareto front, so the right choice depends on which failure a given deployment cares about most. Combining front, side, and distance-to-reference works nicely, but adding rear collisions causes a clear regression. The authors trace this to false positives in the rear-collision metric: the simulator replays other agents from logs, so a log-replayed car that would have braked in reality drives straight into the ego and is scored as the ego's fault. The practical lesson is that the method is only as trustworthy as the metric it upsamples, and a noisy metric can actively steer training in the wrong direction. Distance-to-reference failures, meanwhile, fall from 35 to 28 against the best baseline, about a 20% reduction, and the reweighting leaves inference untouched, so none of this costs anything at drive time. Figure 5 shows a matching qualitative save on the side-collision axis: the baseline drifts off its target trajectory and hits a bus ahead, while the CW-ERM policy slows down behind the bus and avoids the collision.

en.caption: Figure 5. Baseline (top) versus CW-ERM with side collisions upsampled (bottom), over time. The baseline deviates from the target trajectory and collides with the bus ahead (red arrow); CW-ERM slows down behind the bus and prevents the collision.

en.text: A compact scoreboard
The headline comparisons against the strongest baseline are easy to summarize. Each CW-ERM number comes from the variant that upsamples the matching metric.

en.caption: Table 1. CW-ERM versus the best baseline (ERM with perturbation) on the test set. Lower is better.

en.text: Why it matters

The appeal of CW-ERM is how little it asks for. You do not need a differentiable simulator, a human in the loop, or expensive closed-loop training to capture closed-loop benefits. You run your policy once in a simulator, note where it fails, upsample those scenes, and retrain. The recipe delivers meaningful collision reductions, works with any closed-loop metric, and adds no inference latency, since all the extra work happens at training time. The honest boundaries are worth stating too: the gains are measured on one company's proprietary urban dataset, the rear-collision result exposes how sensitive the method is to metric quality, and the simulator's log-replayed agents can manufacture failures that are not really the ego's fault. Even so, as a cheap, metric-agnostic, and theoretically grounded way to nudge an imitation-learned planner toward safer closed-loop behavior, CW-ERM is a genuinely practical idea that a team could adopt without much friction.

zh.text: 如今大多数自动驾驶规划器都用行为克隆（behavioral cloning）来训练：把人类专家的驾驶记录喂给网络，让它去复现专家的下一步动作。训练是开环（open-loop）进行的，一步一步地在离线数据上对齐专家动作。但当策略真正上路时，它是闭环（closed-loop）运行的：它做出的每一个动作都会改变自己下一刻看到的状态。一次微小的转向误差，会把车推到一个专家从未到过的、略微偏移的位置，下一步预测就更差一点，误差不断累积。这就是协变量漂移（covariate shift），也是为什么一个开环指标看起来很漂亮的规划器，仍然可能在路上一路漂移直到发生碰撞。
还有第二个更隐蔽的问题。人们真正在乎的指标，比如有没有碰撞、有没有压线，都是不可微的。训练损失无法直接看到它们，于是开环训练和闭环部署实际上在优化两个不同的目标。一个直接的补救办法，是把仿真器塞进训练回路里、对它做反向传播，像 Urban Driver 这类方法那样。它确实有效，但代价高昂：需要一个可微仿真器，扩展性差，训练时展开策略还非常吃显存。

这篇来自 Woven Planet 的 NeurIPS 2022 论文提出了一个更简单的问题：如果仿真器只用来决定哪些训练场景更重要、而完全不碰损失函数，会怎样？他们的答案就是 CW-ERM（Closed-loop Weighted Empirical Risk Minimization，闭环加权经验风险最小化），一个两步走的配方：找出策略会失败的场景，然后在训练最终策略时，恰恰把这些场景上采样。整套方法都浓缩在下面这张图里。

zh.caption: 图1 CW-ERM 方法总览。步骤 1-2：用普通 ERM 训练一个识别策略。步骤 3-4：在闭环仿真器中回放它，收集代价指标（如碰撞）来构造错误集。步骤 5-6：把错误集中的场景上采样，在加权后的数据上重新训练最终策略。

zh.text: 论文：https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.02174 · 代码：https://github.com/wp-research-uk/cw-erm
为什么开环训练会悄悄拖累闭环驾驶

经验风险最小化（Empirical Risk Minimization，ERM）是标准的行为克隆目标：在专家自身分布采样出的状态上，最小化逐步模仿损失的期望。策略只会被问到专家到访过的状态，因此它从来没有学过如何从自己的错误中恢复。而在部署时分布翻转了，状态现在来自策略自己的滚动轨迹，这两个分布之间的错配，正是让车变得不安全的根源。由于碰撞不可微，ERM 损失并不能给出任何推动策略去规避碰撞的梯度。作者的洞见是：你并不需要一个穿过指标的梯度；你只需要知道策略在哪些场景上出错，而这一点，用一个普通的、不可微的仿真器就能拿到。
方法：三个阶段，一个加权项

CW-ERM 刻意做得很简单，可以拆成三个阶段。第一，用普通方式训练一个识别策略，也就是标准的 ERM 行为克隆。第二，把这个策略放进闭环仿真器，在训练场景上滚动一遍，记录一个代价，比如碰撞次数；每一个代价为正的场景，也就是策略失败的场景，都进入错误集。第三，再次用加权 ERM 训练最终策略，此时错误集里的场景被按因子 w 上采样。最终的目标函数几乎和普通行为克隆一模一样，只多了一个完全由闭环失败驱动的加权项。

有两个实践细节让它真正奏效。识别策略被刻意提前停止，只训练 K 个 epoch，这样它仍然会足够频繁地失败，从而填满一个有意义的错误集；如果训练到收敛，错误集就被掏空了。另外，作者并不是去重新加权损失，而是按一个整数因子把失败场景真正复制上采样，他们发现这样更稳定。因为仿真器只用来给场景打标签、从不用来计算梯度，所以任何不可微指标都能驱动这个加权，也完全不需要可微仿真器。论文还把这种“按失败重加权”的机制，与经典的、通过密度比估计来纠正协变量漂移的思路联系起来，为这个配方给出了一个有原理支撑的骨架。
结果：各项碰撞指标全面下降

方法在一个专有的真实城市驾驶数据集上评估，这些数据由 Woven Planet 的自动驾驶车队在 San Francisco 和 Palo Alto 的高难度任务中采集，包含自车与周围智能体的记录轨迹以及高精地图。场景既难又多样，包括跟停前车、在路口停住、在有行人和骑行者的密集车流中穿行，每段大多持续 11 到 13 秒，最长可达 30 秒。训练用了 180 小时的驾驶数据，另有各 60 小时分别留作验证与测试，最终策略训练 40 个 epoch。闭环仿真器与相关指标已经开源发布。

与最强的基线，也就是带专家扰动的 ERM 行为克隆相比，CW-ERM 在每一项指标上都显著减少了碰撞，其中某些指标的改进达到约 35%。当模型对前向碰撞场景做上采样时，前向碰撞从 14 次降到 9 次，约减少 36%。当它对侧向碰撞场景做上采样时，侧向碰撞从 55 次降到 47 次。这里还有一个可喜的副作用：改进一个指标常常会顺带改进相关指标。对侧向碰撞上采样也降低了后向碰撞，这说明策略是在变得不那么被动谨慎，而不是在钻单一数字的空子。在若干情形下方差也比基线更低，因此这些收益是稳定的，而非侥幸。图2 展示了各指标、各 CW-ERM 变体下的完整对比。

zh.caption: 图2 四项碰撞指标（前向、侧向、后向、到参考轨迹的距离）下的闭环评估。每一行是一个上采样不同指标的 CW-ERM 变体；最上面一行是最强基线（带扰动的 ERM）。误差条为来自精确二项后验（flat prior）的 0.95 置信区间。针对某个指标会压低该指标，而改进往往会外溢到相关指标。

zh.text: 定性行为和总体数字一样说明问题。图3 展示了一个测试场景：基线驶入路口，无视了从右侧驶来的车辆，造成一次前向碰撞；而用前向碰撞场景上采样训练出来的 CW-ERM 策略，则会在路口等待，直到路径清空。这个变化并不是轨迹上的表面微调，而是策略在它过去恰恰会失败的那类情形里，学会了让行。

zh.caption: 图3 一个测试场景，上为基线、下为前向碰撞上采样的 CW-ERM，从左到右是时间推进。蓝点是目标轨迹，黄点是预测轨迹；自车是粉色框，其他智能体是青色框。基线驶入路口，与从右侧来的车相撞（红色箭头）；CW-ERM 则选择等待。

zh.text: 该上采样多少，又该组合哪些指标

有两个旋钮决定这个配方效果好不好。第一个是上采样因子 w。图4 在验证集上把它对侧向碰撞做了扫描：性能稳步改善，直到约 w = 50，此后侧向碰撞又开始回升，这与 Just Train Twice（JTT）方法在其上采样方案中报告的饱和现象如出一辙。第二个旋钮是识别策略的提前停止预算 K：单指标错误集大约 10 个 epoch 最好，多指标错误集则是 20 个。二者合在一起，给出的是一个小而清晰的搜索空间，而不是一个脆弱的空间。

zh.caption: 图4 验证集上侧向碰撞随上采样因子 w 的变化。性能在约 w = 50 之前持续改善，超过之后开始退化；阴影带是置信区间。

zh.text: 此外还有一个选择：该针对哪些失败。对单个指标上采样能在该指标上带来最大收益，而组合多个指标则会沿着帕累托（Pareto）前沿进行权衡，因此具体怎么选，取决于某个部署最在乎的是哪一种失败。把前向、侧向和到参考轨迹的距离组合起来效果不错，但一旦加进后向碰撞就会出现明显的回退。作者把原因追溯到后向碰撞指标里的假阳性：仿真器是从日志回放其他智能体的，因此一辆现实中本会刹车的回放车会径直撞上自车，却被记成自车的过错。这里的实践教训是：方法的可靠程度，取决于它上采样的那个指标有多可靠，一个有噪声的指标反而会把训练带偏。与此同时，到参考轨迹的距离失败相对最强基线从 35 降到 28，约减少 20%，而且这种重加权完全不触碰推理阶段，因此在行车时不会带来任何额外开销。图5 给出了侧向碰撞这一维度上一个对应的定性挽救：基线偏离了目标轨迹、撞上前方的公交车，而 CW-ERM 策略则在公交车后减速，避免了碰撞。

zh.caption: 图5 上为基线、下为侧向碰撞上采样的 CW-ERM，随时间推进。基线偏离目标轨迹，与前方公交车相撞（红色箭头）；CW-ERM 在公交车后减速，避免了碰撞。

zh.text: 一张紧凑的成绩单
针对最强基线的主要对比可以一目了然地总结出来。表中每个 CW-ERM 数字都来自上采样对应指标的那个变体。

zh.caption: 表1 CW-ERM 对比最强基线（带扰动的 ERM）在测试集上的结果，越低越好。
rows: 到参考轨迹距离的失败

zh.text: 为什么它重要

CW-ERM 的吸引力在于它索取得如此之少。你不需要可微仿真器、不需要人在回路，也不需要昂贵的闭环训练，就能拿到闭环带来的好处。你只要在仿真里把策略跑一遍，记下它在哪里失败，把那些场景上采样，然后重新训练。这个配方带来了实实在在的碰撞下降，适用于任何闭环指标，而且不增加任何推理延迟，因为所有额外的开销都发生在训练阶段。诚实的边界也值得一提：这些收益是在某一家公司的专有城市数据集上测得的；后向碰撞的结果暴露出方法对指标质量有多敏感；仿真器里从日志回放的智能体，也可能制造出并不真正归咎于自车的失败。即便如此，作为一种便宜、与指标无关、又有理论支撑的手段，去把一个模仿学习出来的规划器往更安全的闭环行为上推一把，CW-ERM 依然是一个真正实用、团队可以低成本上手的想法。

还有第二个更隐蔽的问题。人们真正在乎的指标，比如有没有碰撞、有没有压线，都是不可微的。训练损失无法直接看到它们，于是开环训练和闭环部署实际上在优化两个不同的目标。一个直接的补救办法，是把仿真器塞进训练回路里、对它做反向传播，像 Urban Driver 这类方法那样。它确实有效，但代价高昂：需要一个可微仿真器，扩展性差，训练时展开策略还非常吃显存。

这篇来自 Woven Planet 的 NeurIPS 2022 论文提出了一个更简单的问题：如果仿真器只用来决定哪些训练场景更重要、而完全不碰损失函数，会怎样？他们的答案就是 CW-ERM（Closed-loop Weighted Empirical Risk Minimization，闭环加权经验风险最小化），一个两步走的配方：找出策略会失败的场景，然后在训练最终策略时，恰恰把这些场景上采样。整套方法都浓缩在下面这张图里。

zh.caption: 图1 CW-ERM 方法总览。步骤 1-2：用普通 ERM 训练一个识别策略。步骤 3-4：在闭环仿真器中回放它，收集代价指标（如碰撞）来构造错误集。步骤 5-6：把错误集中的场景上采样，在加权后的数据上重新训练最终策略。

en.title: NeurIPS 2022 | Train on Your Own Mistakes: A Simple Fix for the Open-Loop/Closed-Loop Gap in Self-Driving
en.subtitle: Woven Planet's CW-ERM runs a policy once in a simulator, finds the scenes where it fails, upsamples them, and retrains, cutting collisions by up to ~35% with no differentiable simulator.

zh.title: NeurIPS 2022 | 让模型在自己的错误上再训练一次：自动驾驶开环/闭环鸿沟的一个简单解法
zh.subtitle: Woven Planet 提出 CW-ERM：先在仿真里跑一遍策略，找出翻车的场景，把它们上采样后重新训练，某些指标上碰撞最多减少约 35%，且无需可微仿真器。

en.caption: Figure 1. High-level overview of CW-ERM. Steps 1-2: train an identification policy with ordinary ERM. Step 3-4: roll it out in a closed-loop simulator and collect a cost metric (e.g. collisions) to build the error set. Steps 5-6: upsample the error-set scenes and retrain the final policy on the reweighted data.

en.text: Why open-loop training quietly hurts closed-loop driving

Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) is the standard behavioral-cloning objective: minimize the expected per-step imitation loss over states drawn from the expert's own distribution. The policy is only ever asked about states the expert visited, so it never learns to recover from its own mistakes. At deployment the distribution flips, since the states are now drawn from the policy's own rollouts, and the mismatch between these two distributions is precisely what makes the car unsafe. Because collisions are non-differentiable, the ERM loss offers no gradient that pushes the policy toward avoiding them. The authors' insight is that you do not need a gradient through the metric; you only need to know which scenes the policy gets wrong, and you can get that from a plain, non-differentiable simulator.

zh.caption: 图1 CW-ERM 方法总览。步骤 1-2：用普通 ERM 训练一个识别策略。步骤 3-4：在闭环仿真器中回放它，收集代价指标（如碰撞）来构造错误集。步骤 5-6：把错误集中的场景上采样，在加权后的数据上重新训练最终策略。

zh.text: 为什么开环训练会悄悄拖累闭环驾驶

经验风险最小化（Empirical Risk Minimization，ERM）是标准的行为克隆目标：在专家自身分布采样出的状态上，最小化逐步模仿损失的期望。策略只会被问到专家到访过的状态，因此它从来没有学过如何从自己的错误中恢复。而在部署时分布翻转了，状态现在来自策略自己的滚动轨迹，这两个分布之间的错配，正是让车变得不安全的根源。由于碰撞不可微，ERM 损失并不能给出任何推动策略去规避碰撞的梯度。作者的洞见是：你并不需要一个穿过指标的梯度；你只需要知道策略在哪些场景上出错，而这一点，用一个普通的、不可微的仿真器就能拿到。

en.title: NeurIPS 2022 | Train on Your Own Mistakes: A Simple Fix for the Open-Loop/Closed-Loop Gap in Self-Driving
en.subtitle: Woven Planet's CW-ERM runs a policy once in a simulator, finds the scenes where it fails, upsamples them, and retrains, cutting collisions by up to ~35% with no differentiable simulator.

zh.title: NeurIPS 2022 | 让模型在自己的错误上再训练一次：自动驾驶开环/闭环鸿沟的一个简单解法
zh.subtitle: Woven Planet 提出 CW-ERM：先在仿真里跑一遍策略，找出翻车的场景，把它们上采样后重新训练，某些指标上碰撞最多减少约 35%，且无需可微仿真器。

en.text: How hard to upsample, and which metrics to combine

Two knobs govern how well the recipe works. The first is the upsampling factor w. Figure 4 sweeps it against side collisions on the validation set: performance improves steadily up to about w = 50, after which side collisions start to climb again, the same saturation the Just Train Twice (JTT) method reports for its upsampling scheme. The second knob is the early-stopping budget K of the identification policy: about 10 epochs works best for single-metric error sets and 20 for multi-metric ones. Together these give a small, legible search space rather than a fragile one.

en.caption: Figure 4. Side collisions on the validation set as a function of the upsampling factor w. Performance improves up to about w = 50 and degrades beyond it; the shaded band is the confidence interval.

en.text: There is also a choice of which failures to target. Upsampling a single metric gives the largest gain on that metric, while combining metrics trades them off along a Pareto front, so the right choice depends on which failure a given deployment cares about most. Combining front, side, and distance-to-reference works nicely, but adding rear collisions causes a clear regression. The authors trace this to false positives in the rear-collision metric: the simulator replays other agents from logs, so a log-replayed car that would have braked in reality drives straight into the ego and is scored as the ego's fault. The practical lesson is that the method is only as trustworthy as the metric it upsamples, and a noisy metric can actively steer training in the wrong direction. Distance-to-reference failures, meanwhile, fall from 35 to 28 against the best baseline, about a 20% reduction, and the reweighting leaves inference untouched, so none of this costs anything at drive time. Figure 5 shows a matching qualitative save on the side-collision axis: the baseline drifts off its target trajectory and hits a bus ahead, while the CW-ERM policy slows down behind the bus and avoids the collision.

en.caption: Figure 5. Baseline (top) versus CW-ERM with side collisions upsampled (bottom), over time. The baseline deviates from the target trajectory and collides with the bus ahead (red arrow); CW-ERM slows down behind the bus and prevents the collision.

zh.caption: 图1 CW-ERM 方法总览。步骤 1-2：用普通 ERM 训练一个识别策略。步骤 3-4：在闭环仿真器中回放它，收集代价指标（如碰撞）来构造错误集。步骤 5-6：把错误集中的场景上采样，在加权后的数据上重新训练最终策略。

zh.text: 方法：三个阶段，一个加权项

CW-ERM 刻意做得很简单，可以拆成三个阶段。第一，用普通方式训练一个识别策略，也就是标准的 ERM 行为克隆。第二，把这个策略放进闭环仿真器，在训练场景上滚动一遍，记录一个代价，比如碰撞次数；每一个代价为正的场景，也就是策略失败的场景，都进入错误集。第三，再次用加权 ERM 训练最终策略，此时错误集里的场景被按因子 w 上采样。最终的目标函数几乎和普通行为克隆一模一样，只多了一个完全由闭环失败驱动的加权项。

有两个实践细节让它真正奏效。识别策略被刻意提前停止，只训练 K 个 epoch，这样它仍然会足够频繁地失败，从而填满一个有意义的错误集；如果训练到收敛，错误集就被掏空了。另外，作者并不是去重新加权损失，而是按一个整数因子把失败场景真正复制上采样，他们发现这样更稳定。因为仿真器只用来给场景打标签、从不用来计算梯度，所以任何不可微指标都能驱动这个加权，也完全不需要可微仿真器。论文还把这种“按失败重加权”的机制，与经典的、通过密度比估计来纠正协变量漂移的思路联系起来，为这个配方给出了一个有原理支撑的骨架。

en.subtitle: Woven Planet's CW-ERM runs a policy once in a simulator, finds the scenes where it fails, upsamples them, and retrains, cutting collisions by up to ~35% with no differentiable simulator.

zh.title: NeurIPS 2022 | 让模型在自己的错误上再训练一次：自动驾驶开环/闭环鸿沟的一个简单解法
zh.subtitle: Woven Planet 提出 CW-ERM：先在仿真里跑一遍策略，找出翻车的场景，把它们上采样后重新训练，某些指标上碰撞最多减少约 35%，且无需可微仿真器。

en.text: Most self-driving planners are trained by behavioral cloning: show the network what a human expert did, and ask it to reproduce the expert's next action. The training is done open-loop, one step at a time, matching expert actions on logged data. But when the policy actually drives, it runs closed-loop: every action it takes changes the state it sees next. A small steering error nudges the car into a slightly off-center position the expert never visited, the next prediction is a little worse, and the errors compound. This is covariate shift, and it is why a planner that looks excellent on open-loop metrics can still drift into collisions on the road.

There is a second, quieter problem. The metrics people actually care about (did the car collide, did it leave its lane) are non-differentiable. The training loss cannot see them directly, so open-loop training and closed-loop deployment end up optimizing two different objectives. The obvious remedy is to put a simulator inside the training loop and backpropagate through it, as methods like Urban Driver do. It works, but it is expensive: it needs a differentiable simulator, it does not scale well, and unrolling the policy during training is memory-hungry.

This NeurIPS 2022 paper from Woven Planet asks a simpler question. What if the simulator is used only to decide which training scenes matter, and never touches the loss function? Their answer is CW-ERM, or Closed-loop Weighted Empirical Risk Minimization: a two-step recipe that finds the scenes a policy fails on and upsamples exactly those scenes when training the final policy. The whole method is captured in the figure below.

en.caption: Figure 1. High-level overview of CW-ERM. Steps 1-2: train an identification policy with ordinary ERM. Step 3-4: roll it out in a closed-loop simulator and collect a cost metric (e.g. collisions) to build the error set. Steps 5-6: upsample the error-set scenes and retrain the final policy on the reweighted data.

en.text: Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.02174 · Code: https://github.com/wp-research-uk/cw-erm
The method: three stages, one weighting term

CW-ERM is deliberately simple and breaks into three stages. First, train an identification policy the ordinary way, with standard ERM behavioral cloning. Second, roll that policy out in a closed-loop simulator across the training scenes and record a cost such as the number of collisions; every scene where the cost is positive, meaning every scene the policy fails, goes into an error set. Third, train the final policy again with weighted ERM, where the error-set scenes are upsampled by a factor w. The final objective is almost identical to plain behavioral cloning, with the single addition of a weight that is driven entirely by closed-loop failures.

Two practical details make it work. The identification policy is stopped early, after K epochs, so that it still fails often enough to populate a meaningful error set; train it to convergence and the error set is depleted. And rather than reweighting the loss, the authors physically upsample the failing scenes by an integer factor, which they find more stable. Because the simulator is used only to label scenes and never to compute a gradient, any non-differentiable metric can drive the weighting, and no differentiable simulator is needed. The paper also connects this reweight-by-failure scheme to the classic idea of correcting covariate shift through density-ratio estimation, giving the recipe a principled backbone.

en.title: NeurIPS 2022 | Train on Your Own Mistakes: A Simple Fix for the Open-Loop/Closed-Loop Gap in Self-Driving
en.subtitle: Woven Planet's CW-ERM runs a policy once in a simulator, finds the scenes where it fails, upsamples them, and retrains, cutting collisions by up to ~35% with no differentiable simulator.

zh.title: NeurIPS 2022 | 让模型在自己的错误上再训练一次：自动驾驶开环/闭环鸿沟的一个简单解法
zh.subtitle: Woven Planet 提出 CW-ERM：先在仿真里跑一遍策略，找出翻车的场景，把它们上采样后重新训练，某些指标上碰撞最多减少约 35%，且无需可微仿真器。

en.text: Results: fewer collisions across the board

The method is evaluated on a proprietary real-world urban driving dataset collected by Woven Planet's self-driving cars on challenging missions in San Francisco and Palo Alto, complete with recorded ego and agent trajectories and HD maps. The scenes are hard and varied (stopping behind a lead vehicle, holding at intersections, threading dense traffic with pedestrians and cyclists) and run 11 to 13 seconds each, up to 30 seconds at the longest. Training uses 180 hours of driving, with 60 hours each held out for validation and test, and the final policy is trained for 40 epochs. The closed-loop simulator and metrics are released as open source.

Compared against the strongest baseline, behavioral cloning with ERM and expert perturbation, CW-ERM reduces collisions significantly across every metric, with improvements reaching about 35% on some of them. When the model upsamples front-collision scenes, front collisions fall from 14 to 9, roughly a 36% reduction. When it upsamples side-collision scenes, side collisions fall from 55 to 47. There is a welcome side effect: improving one metric often improves related ones. Upsampling side collisions also reduces rear collisions, a sign that the policy is becoming less passively cautious rather than gaming a single number. Variance is also lower than the baseline in several cases, so the gains are stable rather than lucky. Figure 2 shows the full picture across metrics and CW-ERM variants.

en.caption: Figure 2. Closed-loop evaluation across four collision metrics (front, side, rear, distance-to-reference). Each row is a CW-ERM variant that upsamples a different metric; the top row is the best baseline (ERM with perturbation). Bars show 0.95 confidence intervals from an exact Binomial posterior. Targeting a metric shrinks it, and improvements often carry over to related metrics.

en.text: The qualitative behavior is just as telling as the aggregate numbers. Figure 3 shows a test scene where the baseline drives into an intersection, ignores a car approaching from the right, and causes a front collision; the CW-ERM policy, trained with front-collision scenes upsampled, instead waits at the intersection until the path is clear. The change is not a cosmetic trajectory tweak: it is the policy learning to yield in exactly the situation type it used to fail on.

en.caption: Figure 3. A test scene, baseline (top) versus CW-ERM with front collisions upsampled (bottom), left to right in time. Blue dots are the target trajectory, yellow dots the prediction; the ego is the pink box, other agents the teal boxes. The baseline enters the intersection and collides with the car from the right (red arrow); CW-ERM waits instead.

zh.text: 结果：各项碰撞指标全面下降

方法在一个专有的真实城市驾驶数据集上评估，这些数据由 Woven Planet 的自动驾驶车队在 San Francisco 和 Palo Alto 的高难度任务中采集，包含自车与周围智能体的记录轨迹以及高精地图。场景既难又多样，包括跟停前车、在路口停住、在有行人和骑行者的密集车流中穿行，每段大多持续 11 到 13 秒，最长可达 30 秒。训练用了 180 小时的驾驶数据，另有各 60 小时分别留作验证与测试，最终策略训练 40 个 epoch。闭环仿真器与相关指标已经开源发布。

与最强的基线，也就是带专家扰动的 ERM 行为克隆相比，CW-ERM 在每一项指标上都显著减少了碰撞，其中某些指标的改进达到约 35%。当模型对前向碰撞场景做上采样时，前向碰撞从 14 次降到 9 次，约减少 36%。当它对侧向碰撞场景做上采样时，侧向碰撞从 55 次降到 47 次。这里还有一个可喜的副作用：改进一个指标常常会顺带改进相关指标。对侧向碰撞上采样也降低了后向碰撞，这说明策略是在变得不那么被动谨慎，而不是在钻单一数字的空子。在若干情形下方差也比基线更低，因此这些收益是稳定的，而非侥幸。图2 展示了各指标、各 CW-ERM 变体下的完整对比。

zh.caption: 图2 四项碰撞指标（前向、侧向、后向、到参考轨迹的距离）下的闭环评估。每一行是一个上采样不同指标的 CW-ERM 变体；最上面一行是最强基线（带扰动的 ERM）。误差条为来自精确二项后验（flat prior）的 0.95 置信区间。针对某个指标会压低该指标，而改进往往会外溢到相关指标。

zh.text: 定性行为和总体数字一样说明问题。图3 展示了一个测试场景：基线驶入路口，无视了从右侧驶来的车辆，造成一次前向碰撞；而用前向碰撞场景上采样训练出来的 CW-ERM 策略，则会在路口等待，直到路径清空。这个变化并不是轨迹上的表面微调，而是策略在它过去恰恰会失败的那类情形里，学会了让行。

zh.caption: 图3 一个测试场景，上为基线、下为前向碰撞上采样的 CW-ERM，从左到右是时间推进。蓝点是目标轨迹，黄点是预测轨迹；自车是粉色框，其他智能体是青色框。基线驶入路口，与从右侧来的车相撞（红色箭头）；CW-ERM 则选择等待。

zh.title: NeurIPS 2022 | 让模型在自己的错误上再训练一次：自动驾驶开环/闭环鸿沟的一个简单解法
zh.subtitle: Woven Planet 提出 CW-ERM：先在仿真里跑一遍策略，找出翻车的场景，把它们上采样后重新训练，某些指标上碰撞最多减少约 35%，且无需可微仿真器。

en.text: Results: fewer collisions across the board

The method is evaluated on a proprietary real-world urban driving dataset collected by Woven Planet's self-driving cars on challenging missions in San Francisco and Palo Alto, complete with recorded ego and agent trajectories and HD maps. The scenes are hard and varied (stopping behind a lead vehicle, holding at intersections, threading dense traffic with pedestrians and cyclists) and run 11 to 13 seconds each, up to 30 seconds at the longest. Training uses 180 hours of driving, with 60 hours each held out for validation and test, and the final policy is trained for 40 epochs. The closed-loop simulator and metrics are released as open source.

Compared against the strongest baseline, behavioral cloning with ERM and expert perturbation, CW-ERM reduces collisions significantly across every metric, with improvements reaching about 35% on some of them. When the model upsamples front-collision scenes, front collisions fall from 14 to 9, roughly a 36% reduction. When it upsamples side-collision scenes, side collisions fall from 55 to 47. There is a welcome side effect: improving one metric often improves related ones. Upsampling side collisions also reduces rear collisions, a sign that the policy is becoming less passively cautious rather than gaming a single number. Variance is also lower than the baseline in several cases, so the gains are stable rather than lucky. Figure 2 shows the full picture across metrics and CW-ERM variants.

en.caption: Figure 2. Closed-loop evaluation across four collision metrics (front, side, rear, distance-to-reference). Each row is a CW-ERM variant that upsamples a different metric; the top row is the best baseline (ERM with perturbation). Bars show 0.95 confidence intervals from an exact Binomial posterior. Targeting a metric shrinks it, and improvements often carry over to related metrics.

en.text: The qualitative behavior is just as telling as the aggregate numbers. Figure 3 shows a test scene where the baseline drives into an intersection, ignores a car approaching from the right, and causes a front collision; the CW-ERM policy, trained with front-collision scenes upsampled, instead waits at the intersection until the path is clear. The change is not a cosmetic trajectory tweak: it is the policy learning to yield in exactly the situation type it used to fail on.

en.caption: Figure 3. A test scene, baseline (top) versus CW-ERM with front collisions upsampled (bottom), left to right in time. Blue dots are the target trajectory, yellow dots the prediction; the ego is the pink box, other agents the teal boxes. The baseline enters the intersection and collides with the car from the right (red arrow); CW-ERM waits instead.

en.text: Why it matters

The appeal of CW-ERM is how little it asks for. You do not need a differentiable simulator, a human in the loop, or expensive closed-loop training to capture closed-loop benefits. You run your policy once in a simulator, note where it fails, upsample those scenes, and retrain. The recipe delivers meaningful collision reductions, works with any closed-loop metric, and adds no inference latency, since all the extra work happens at training time. The honest boundaries are worth stating too: the gains are measured on one company's proprietary urban dataset, the rear-collision result exposes how sensitive the method is to metric quality, and the simulator's log-replayed agents can manufacture failures that are not really the ego's fault. Even so, as a cheap, metric-agnostic, and theoretically grounded way to nudge an imitation-learned planner toward safer closed-loop behavior, CW-ERM is a genuinely practical idea that a team could adopt without much friction.

zh.text: 为什么它重要

CW-ERM 的吸引力在于它索取得如此之少。你不需要可微仿真器、不需要人在回路，也不需要昂贵的闭环训练，就能拿到闭环带来的好处。你只要在仿真里把策略跑一遍，记下它在哪里失败，把那些场景上采样，然后重新训练。这个配方带来了实实在在的碰撞下降，适用于任何闭环指标，而且不增加任何推理延迟，因为所有额外的开销都发生在训练阶段。诚实的边界也值得一提：这些收益是在某一家公司的专有城市数据集上测得的；后向碰撞的结果暴露出方法对指标质量有多敏感；仿真器里从日志回放的智能体，也可能制造出并不真正归咎于自车的失败。即便如此，作为一种便宜、与指标无关、又有理论支撑的手段，去把一个模仿学习出来的规划器往更安全的闭环行为上推一把，CW-ERM 依然是一个真正实用、团队可以低成本上手的想法。

zh.subtitle: Woven Planet 提出 CW-ERM：先在仿真里跑一遍策略，找出翻车的场景，把它们上采样后重新训练，某些指标上碰撞最多减少约 35%，且无需可微仿真器。

en.caption: Figure 1. High-level overview of CW-ERM. Steps 1-2: train an identification policy with ordinary ERM. Step 3-4: roll it out in a closed-loop simulator and collect a cost metric (e.g. collisions) to build the error set. Steps 5-6: upsample the error-set scenes and retrain the final policy on the reweighted data.

en.text: Why open-loop training quietly hurts closed-loop driving

Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) is the standard behavioral-cloning objective: minimize the expected per-step imitation loss over states drawn from the expert's own distribution. The policy is only ever asked about states the expert visited, so it never learns to recover from its own mistakes. At deployment the distribution flips, since the states are now drawn from the policy's own rollouts, and the mismatch between these two distributions is precisely what makes the car unsafe. Because collisions are non-differentiable, the ERM loss offers no gradient that pushes the policy toward avoiding them. The authors' insight is that you do not need a gradient through the metric; you only need to know which scenes the policy gets wrong, and you can get that from a plain, non-differentiable simulator.

zh.caption: 图1 CW-ERM 方法总览。步骤 1-2：用普通 ERM 训练一个识别策略。步骤 3-4：在闭环仿真器中回放它，收集代价指标（如碰撞）来构造错误集。步骤 5-6：把错误集中的场景上采样，在加权后的数据上重新训练最终策略。

zh.text: 为什么开环训练会悄悄拖累闭环驾驶

经验风险最小化（Empirical Risk Minimization，ERM）是标准的行为克隆目标：在专家自身分布采样出的状态上，最小化逐步模仿损失的期望。策略只会被问到专家到访过的状态，因此它从来没有学过如何从自己的错误中恢复。而在部署时分布翻转了，状态现在来自策略自己的滚动轨迹，这两个分布之间的错配，正是让车变得不安全的根源。由于碰撞不可微，ERM 损失并不能给出任何推动策略去规避碰撞的梯度。作者的洞见是：你并不需要一个穿过指标的梯度；你只需要知道策略在哪些场景上出错，而这一点，用一个普通的、不可微的仿真器就能拿到。
